description: Wanderer turns NASA SPHEREx data into a public web tool for watching the sky move. Pick any spot and it pulls every SPHEREx image of it from NASA/IPAC IRSA, lines them up and lets you blink, swipe or flip through time. It finds moving objects, names known asteroids and comets with JPL data, follows comets like 3I/ATLAS and builds spectra. Built with Go, Python and React plus 3D views. We welcome people into astronomy data, design or video storytelling.
summary:
Since 2025, NASA's SPHEREx mission has mapped the entire sky every six months in 102 colours of near-infrared light. Asteroids, comets and nearby fast-moving stars reveal themselves by shifting between those images, but the data are huge and hard to use. Wanderer is a free public web tool that turns them into something anyone can explore.

Pick any spot in the sky and Wanderer pulls every SPHEREx image of it from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, lines them up and lets you blink, swipe, subtract and flip through them over time. It marks the asteroids and comets NASA JPL predicts in each frame, finds what moved by itself, follows named objects such as the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS through dozens of images, builds infrared spectra from many visits, and shows where SPHEREx is right now in 3D.

On real SPHEREx data it detects asteroid 872 Holda moving 8 arcminutes in 44 hours and the fainter 4979 Otawara, both confirmed against JPL. Wanderer makes a cutting-edge sky survey open to students, amateur astronomers and the curious, so more eyes can search the changing sky.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Wanderer is a web application that shows SPHEREx sky images and makes changes over time easy to see.

- Explore: search a name or coordinates, or click a real sky map. See how many SPHEREx images cover the spot, per detector.

- Timeline: every visit on a date versus wavelength chart, with the two six-month survey windows and one-click best image pairs.

- Compare: blink, swipe, side by side, difference image, flipbook and a SPHEREx false-colour view. Frames are rotated north up from their own coordinates so images six months apart line up.

- Known objects: asteroids and comets from NASA JPL's Small-Body Identification service, computed for the exact time of each image, move with the flipbook.

- Find movers: aligns two images, subtracts them, rejects star residue and matches what remains to JPL. Unmatched detections are flagged for a closer look.

- Track: give an asteroid or comet name; Wanderer gets its path from JPL Horizons, finds every SPHEREx image that caught it and plays them as a movie, with its 3D path around the Sun.

- Spectrum: each SPHEREx detector sees a different wavelength across its width, so many visits add up to a spectrum. Wanderer measures the target in each one and draws the spectrum live.

- SPHEREx right now: the observatory's real position over Earth from live orbital elements, and an interactive 3D model of the spacecraft and its six-detector focal plane.

- Focus mode explains every button in a bubble above it. Dark and light themes. Progress is kept between pages. Works on phones.

HOW IT WORKS

A Go gateway handles all archive requests (IRSA Simple Image Access and cutouts, JPL APIs, CDS Sesame, CelesTrak) with retries, caching and background jobs streamed to the browser over WebSockets. A Python science service (astropy, numpy, scipy) reads the FITS files, handles sky coordinates and the wavelength map, aligns images, makes difference images, detects sources and measures brightness. The React and TypeScript front end uses Aladin Lite for the sky map and three.js for 3D. Only small cutouts are downloaded, never the full 66 MB images. Everything runs in Docker behind Caddy with HTTPS, with GitHub Actions CI and automatic, health-checked deployment.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

SPHEREx data are public but technical. Wanderer lets students, teachers, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists see the moving sky in seconds, learn how an infrared survey works, and check candidate movers against known objects. The same pipeline could feed citizen-science searches for new asteroids, comets or nearby brown dwarfs.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It treats the SPHEREx colour-changing filter as a feature instead of a problem: it always shows the wavelength at the target, prefers image pairs at matching wavelengths so blinks are fair, and turns the same effect into spectra and false-colour views.

TOOLS

Go, Python (FastAPI, astropy, numpy, scipy, Pillow), TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, Aladin Lite, satellite.js, Docker, Caddy, GitHub Actions.

SOURCE CODE

https://github.com/fromearth03/wanderer
